t: Introduction: topic and aim of the lesson
n: In this lesson we talk about sudden infant death syndrome, SIDS for short. This is the unexplained death of a child under one year of age in sleep. According to Simpson's definition, the death is unexpected, and the cause is not found even after a full autopsy, review of the circumstances and history. SIDS remains one of the commonest causes of death in the post-neonatal period in developed countries. By the end of the lesson we will understand that the diagnosis of SIDS is made only after other causes have been excluded.

t: SIDS: definition and historical stages
n: Now we look at the definition and historical stages. The term "sudden infant death syndrome" was adopted in 1969 at an international conference; it was the Second International Conference. The old names are "cot death" and "crib death"; in the middle of the last century precisely the term cot death was used. In 1979 the syndrome was included in the International Classification of Diseases. That is, sudden death of a child under one year in sleep, if the cause is not found even on full examination, is regarded as SIDS.

t: SIDS hypotheses: mechanical, allergic, thymic, infectious
n: There are four SIDS hypotheses: mechanical, allergic, thymic and infectious. The mechanical hypothesis says that the child is smothered by a sheet, blanket or pillow. The allergic hypothesis assumes a reaction to cow's milk proteins. The thymic hypothesis proposes that an enlarged thymus gland compresses. The infectious hypothesis names a fulminant virus or bacterium as the cause. There is no single approach: opinion on the mechanism of death is not united. None of them can fully explain all cases of SIDS. Attention: a hypothesis is not a proven cause, and the exact cause has still not been found.

t: Respiratory and cardiogenic hypotheses
n: In recent times the origin of SIDS has been explained mainly by the respiratory and cardiogenic hypotheses. The respiratory hypothesis links death with apnoea, that is cessation of breathing; apnoea may be central, peripheral or mixed. The cardiogenic hypothesis, on the other hand, links it with cessation of cardiac activity: a disturbance of the repolarisation process leads to asystole and death. Attention: apnoea and asystole are not the same thing. Both are for now hypotheses, not a single mechanism.

t: Epidemiology of SIDS
n: We dwell on the epidemiology of SIDS. Sudden infant death syndrome takes third place in the structure of causes of infant mortality. In different countries the rate is in the range of 0.5–2.8 per 1000 live births. In Uzbekistan the question is poorly studied; according to studies the rate was assumed to exceed 1.5. SIDS is commoner in premature infants aged 2–6 months, in autumn and winter, in the morning. In twins the rate is several times higher.

t: Simpson: definition and features of SIDS
n: The definition of SIDS according to Simpson: sudden death of a child under 1 year, beginning in sleep and unexplained even after full examination. In developed countries the rate has fallen from about 2 to 0.5 per 1000 live births; in England and Wales in 2007 it was 0.28. The decline coincided with improvement in social and living conditions and with the "Back to Sleep" campaign, that is placing infants on the back, in the early 1990s. Most deaths are at 1–6 months, with a peak at 2 months; commoner in twins; markedly commoner in cold and damp months.

t: Risk factors for SIDS: after Simpson
n: Risk factors for SIDS after Simpson. Most deaths are at 1–6 months, with a peak at 2 months; somewhat more in boys. In multiple births, that is twins, the risk is markedly higher, partly because of premature birth and low weight. In a temperate climate, SIDS is much commoner in cold and damp months. Social and racial differences are explained by socio-economic factors; however, no social stratum is an exception. It is recommended that the mother not smoke during pregnancy and after delivery, and that the child not be overwrapped.

t: Risk factors for SIDS
n: We divide the risk factors into groups. By sleeping place: no separate bed, sleeping with the mother. By sleeping method: tight swaddling and placing on the stomach. Social and living factors: unsatisfactory conditions, low education. By pregnancy: pathological course and lack of supervision. Overheating and sleeping on the stomach also raise the risk. Young maternal age, smoking, and alcohol and narcotic use also raise the risk. A short interval between births also raises the risk. Eliminating the factors reduces mortality.

t: Prevention: infants are not doomed
n: An important idea from the point of view of prevention: infants are not doomed to die. Eliminating risk factors considerably lowers the probability of death. Infants with risk factors cannot be regarded as doomed to die. With proper care and medical supervision, the infant passes through the dangerous period in good health and grows up healthy. Remember: the dangerous period is the first year of life, especially the first 6 months.

t: Preparing for the examination: documents and follow-up history
n: Preparation for the examination begins before examination of the corpse. First all medical documents are carefully studied. Then a follow-up history is taken from the parents: inquiry is made about birth, development and family circumstances, and also about ALTE episodes. After that, one proceeds to examination of the corpse. Remember: in SIDS, in 15–20 per cent there are mild respiratory signs.

t: Findings on examination of the corpse in SIDS
n: Findings on examination of the corpse in SIDS. On external examination there are haemorrhages in the conjunctivae of the eyes and eyelids, and cadaveric lividity is abundant and appears quickly. In the internal organs congestion, liquid blood and petechiae are found. Under the microscope emphysema and foci of atelectasis are seen. On internal examination, small haemorrhages are found under the visceral pleura and epicardium. In 15–25 per cent a thymico-lymphatic state occurs: the thymus and lymph nodes are enlarged. Sometimes a runny liquid mass is found in the trachea and bronchi; it is explained by gastro-oesophageal reflux.

t: Simpson: findings and theories of SIDS
n: The essence of SIDS according to Simpson is that the death is unexpected, and on thorough examination an adequate cause is not found. In about 70 per cent of cases there are intrathoracic petechiae on the pleura, epicardium and thymus; this is an agonal phenomenon, not the cause of death. None of the theories — cow's milk allergy, prolonged apnoea, hyperthermia, CO poisoning — has been proven. The supposition of deliberate smothering by parents, that is up to 10 per cent, has never been proven. The main task is support of the family.

t: History and autopsy: what is found
n: About the history and autopsy. The usual history is as follows: a completely healthy child, or one with mild symptoms, is put to sleep in the evening and found dead in the morning. At autopsy in true SIDS nothing specific is found. In about 70 per cent of cases there are petechiae on the pleura, epicardium and thymus. Petechiae were previously wrongly interpreted as mechanical suffocation; now they are regarded as an agonal phenomenon, not the cause of death.

t: Aetiology: multifactorial and unproven theories
n: The aetiology is multifactorial and rests on unproven theories. The true cause of SIDS is unknown; probably there are many causes, acting through a common final pathway, that is cardiorespiratory failure. The theories proposed: cow's milk allergy, prolonged apnoea, metabolic defects, hyperthermia, hypothermia, CO or CO2 poisoning, viral bronchiolitis. Abnormal development of the cardiorespiratory control centres in the brainstem has also been pointed out; so far none has been proven. As in sudden unexplained death in adults, in some cases the cause may be found by the methods of molecular biology.

t: Age distribution of infant deaths
n: We look at the age distribution of infant deaths. Of sudden infant deaths from respiratory diseases, 80 per cent occur in the first half-year of life. In the second half of the first year, 12 per cent of these cases are seen, and the rest occur after one year. Attention: this share relates to respiratory diseases, not to sudden infant death syndrome, that is SIDS.

t: Thymico-lymphatic state
n: In the thymico-lymphatic state the thymus and lymph nodes are enlarged, while the adrenal glands are insufficiently developed, that is hypoplasia is seen. Such children are sensitive to influences: even a not very strong external or internal influence causes an excessively strong response. During life this state is detected only on targeted in-depth examination. Often it is an incidental finding in the corpse.

t: Over-diagnosis of pneumonia
n: About over-diagnosis of pneumonia. The share of pneumonia among causes of child deaths is still artificially inflated; this is called over-diagnosis. The main reason: the doctor does not examine the sick child carefully, and the necessary laboratory and instrumental examinations are not carried out. Even if pneumonia is reliably established, it is not always the main cause of death. Attention: pneumonia is not the same as the cause of death. In most cases, that is in 60–75%, it is a competing cause, a complication or a concomitant disease.

t: Case analysis: diagnosis of pneumonia in an infant
n: Case analysis. Situation: in the medical documents of a dead infant pneumonia is reliably established. Question: may it be recorded as the main cause of death? Answer: not always. In most cases, that is in 60–75%, pneumonia is not the main cause but a competing cause, a complication or a concomitant disease. The doctor must give in the medical documents information on the mechanism of death. A conclusion of "pneumonia" without careful examination artificially inflates its share, that is leads to over-diagnosis.

t: Diagnosis of SIDS and errors of under-diagnosis
n: The diagnosis of SIDS is made only after other conditions that could lead to death have been excluded. Attention: SIDS is not pneumonia or asphyxia, but it is often wrongly labelled so; this is under-diagnosis. Erroneous interpretations: when bronchopneumonia is stated, the change in the lung is insufficient for death; when mechanical asphyxia is stated, signs of rapid death occur in SIDS too; when airway obstruction is stated, a small amount of material may be the result of reflux. Such an error may lead to paediatricians being unjustifiably held liable, including criminally.

t: Attention: distinguishing SIDS from mechanical asphyxia
n: It is important to distinguish SIDS from mechanical asphyxia. Signs of rapid death occur in both, so they cannot be the sole basis. In SIDS the small amount of material in the trachea is reflux, and the conclusion rests on exclusion of other causes. If one follows the circumstances of the case blindly, the findings in the corpse are wrongly interpreted. Remember: a small amount of gastric material in the trachea does not mean that the airway was obstructed.

t: Distinguishing SIDS from child abuse: bruises
n: Now we move to distinguishing SIDS from child abuse, first by bruises. Deaths from abuse are commoner up to 2 years; the commonest method of death is head injury. In a bruise, what matters is: location, age and number. Bruises on the face, ear, lip, neck, side of the chest, anterior abdominal wall, buttock and thigh require explanation. Soft tissue bruising in an immobile infant, imprints of objects and many bruises of the same shape point to abuse. The explanations of the carers are carefully recorded and their change over time is compared.

t: Excluding abuse: skeletal injury
n: In excluding abuse, skeletal injury is also examined. If abuse is suspected up to 2 years, a whole-body X-ray examination is performed by the standard protocol. Healed fractures show episodes of earlier injury; histological assessment is more precise. A rib fracture is rarely accidental in children; callus on the posterior ribs gives a "rosary" appearance. Skull fractures that are multiple, bilateral or cross sutures are more characteristic of abuse.

t: Case analysis: infant death on a pillow
n: Case analysis on infant death on a pillow. Situation: a breastfeeding mother fell asleep and the infant beside her died; or the infant lies turned over on a pillow and has become stiff. On the corpse, congestion of the internal organs, liquid blood and small haemorrhages are found; these occur in asphyxia too. The conclusion must rely on medical documents, follow-up history from the parents and laboratory results. Question: how will you justify the diagnosis if no other disease or trauma is found? SIDS is then diagnosed by exclusion.

t: Working with parents in SIDS
n: Working with the parents in SIDS requires special attention. In any child death the health worker must be vigilant. The risk of intensifying the irreparable sense of guilt in innocent parents is weighed against the possibility of detecting deliberate smothering. The supposition of deliberate smothering by parents, that is up to 10 per cent, has never been proven. The main task is to support the family with explanations and to ensure use of counselling services.

t: Conclusion and review questions
n: We summarise. SIDS is the unexpected death of a child under one year in sleep, the cause of which is not found even after full examination. It is commonest at 1–6 months, with a peak at 2 months; the decline is related to "Back to Sleep" and the improvement in social and living conditions. The diagnosis is made after other causes, that is pneumonia, mechanical asphyxia and abuse, have been excluded. Petechiae are an agonal phenomenon and not the cause of death.
